The electrostatic force is **conservative**, so the work done round any **closed** path
is zero.
**Step 1 — note the geometry.** The charge q travels once round a circle centred on Q,
so every point of the path is at the **same distance r** from Q ✓
**Step 2 — look at the potential.** The potential at distance r is
V = Q/(4πε₀r)
and since r never changes, **V is constant** all the way round ✓
**Step 3 — compute the work.**
W = q(V_initial − V_final)
= q(V − V)
= **0** ✓
**The force-and-displacement view.** The Coulomb force on q is **radial**, directed along
the line joining it to Q ✓ The motion along a circle is **tangential** - always
perpendicular to that radius. With F̄ ⟂ d̄s̄ at every point,
W = ∫F̄·d̄s̄ = ∫F ds cos 90° = **0** ✓
**Why this holds for any closed path, not just a circle.** The electrostatic field is
**conservative**, so the work depends only on the **endpoints** ✓ For a closed loop the
endpoints coincide, and the work is zero whatever route is taken - a square, an
irregular wiggle, or a circle not centred on Q.
**The circulation statement of the same fact.**
∮ Ē·d̄l̄ = **0** ✓
This is one of the basic properties of an electrostatic field, and it is what allows a
**potential** to be defined at all. A field with non-zero circulation - such as the
induced electric field around a changing magnetic flux - has no single-valued potential.
**Why "none of these" is the answer.** The three expressions offered are all non-zero
energies built from q, Q and r ✓ The first, qQ/(4πε₀r), is the potential energy of the
pair at separation r - a real quantity, but not the **work done** in going round the
loop, which is zero.
**A practical illustration.** Carrying a charge once round an equipotential costs
nothing ✓ just as carrying a weight once round a level contour on a hillside does no
work against gravity.
∴ none of these - the work done is zero.

Coulomb's law governs **electric** forces; the binding of protons and neutrons is the
work of the **strong nuclear force**.
**Step 1 — test each statement.**
"**binds electrons to the nucleus**" ✓ **true** - the attraction between the negative
electron and the positive nucleus is purely electrostatic.
"**binds atoms into molecules**" ✓ **true** - covalent and ionic bonds are
electromagnetic in origin, arising from the attraction of electrons for nuclei.
"**binds atoms and molecules into solids**" ✓ **true** - metallic, ionic and van der
Waals bonding are all electrical.
"**binds protons and neutrons in the nucleus**" ✗ **false** - this is the statement to
pick ✓
**Step 2 — see why the nuclear case fails.** Within a nucleus the protons **repel** each
other electrostatically, and fiercely: at a separation of 10⁻¹⁵ m the Coulomb repulsion
between two protons is about **230 N** ✓ Were that the only force, no nucleus beyond
hydrogen could exist for an instant.
**Step 3 — name the force that does the binding.** The **strong nuclear force** ✓ It is
about **100 times** stronger than the electrostatic force at nuclear distances, acts
equally between protons and neutrons, and is **charge-independent**. It also has a very
short range - about 10⁻¹⁵ m - beyond which it vanishes.
**Why neutrons settle the matter.** A neutron is **uncharged**, so Coulomb's law gives
**no force at all** on it ✓ Yet neutrons are bound in nuclei as tightly as protons -
decisive evidence that some other force is at work.
**How the two forces compete in a nucleus.** The strong force reaches only to
neighbouring nucleons, while the electrostatic repulsion acts across the **whole**
nucleus ✓ As Z grows the repulsion accumulates faster than the attraction, which is why
heavy nuclei need extra neutrons and why nothing beyond about Z = 83 is stable.
**The four fundamental forces, for perspective.** Strong, electromagnetic, weak,
gravitational ✓ Coulomb's law is the electrostatic part of the second; nuclear binding
belongs to the first.
∴ the statement that Coulomb's law binds the protons and neutrons in the nucleus.

The electric field is **minus the gradient** of the potential.
**Step 1 — write the relation.** With V depending only on x,
E_x = −dV/dx ✓
**Step 2 — differentiate V = 3x² + 5.**
dV/dx = **6x**
so
E_x = **−6x**
**Step 3 — evaluate at the given point.** Only the x coordinate matters, and it is
**−2 m**:
E = −6(−2)
= **+12 V m⁻¹** ✓
**Why y and z are irrelevant.** V contains no y or z, so
E_y = −∂V/∂y = **0** and E_z = **0** ✓
The field points entirely along x, and the coordinates 1 and 0 are given only to see
whether that is recognised.
**Why the constant 5 disappears.** It shifts the potential everywhere by the same
amount, and a uniform shift produces no field ✓ Only **differences** of potential have
physical meaning - which is why the zero of potential may be chosen freely.
**What the sign means.** A positive E_x means the field points along **+x** ✓ Since
V = 3x² is smallest at x = 0, the field everywhere points **towards** the origin from the
positive side and away from it on the negative side - always from high potential to low.
**A check by finite differences.** Near x = −2:
V(−2·01) = 3(4·0401) + 5 = **17·12 V**
V(−1·99) = 3(3·9601) + 5 = **16·88 V**
E_x = −ΔV/Δx = −(16·88 − 17·12)/0·02 = **+12 V m⁻¹** ✓ exactly.
**Checking the units.** V is in volts and x in metres, so dV/dx is in **V m⁻¹** ✓ the
correct unit for a field, equivalent to N C⁻¹.
**Reading the distractors.** **−12 V m⁻¹** ✗ is the commonest slip - forgetting that
x = −2 is itself negative, so that −6x comes out **positive**. **±17 V m⁻¹** ✗ come from
evaluating V rather than its derivative: V(−2) = 17 V ✓ which is the potential, not the
field.
∴ +12 Vm⁻¹.

Reduce the network, find the total charge, then share it between the parallel pair.
**Step 1 — combine the parallel capacitors.** The 4 µF and 2 µF are across the same two
nodes:
C_parallel = 4 + 2 = **6 µF** ✓
**Step 2 — combine with the 6 µF in series.**
1/C_total = 1/6 + 1/6 = 2/6
**C_total = 3 µF** ✓
**Step 3 — find the total charge drawn from the battery.**
Q = C_total V
= 3 x 10⁻⁶ x 12
= **36 x 10⁻⁶ C** ✓
This is the charge on the 6 µF capacitor, since it carries the whole current in series.
**Step 4 — share that charge between the parallel pair.** They have the same voltage, so
the charge divides in proportion to the capacitances:
Q₄ = 36 µC x 4/(4 + 2)
= 36 x (2/3)
= **24 x 10⁻⁶ C** ✓
**A check by voltages.** The series pair are both 6 µF, so the 12 V divides **equally**:
**6 V** across the 6 µF and **6 V** across the parallel combination ✓
then
Q₄ = C V = 4 µF x 6 V = **24 µC** ✓
Q₂ = 2 µF x 6 V = **12 µC**
and 24 + 12 = **36 µC** ✓ matching the charge on the 6 µF capacitor.
**Why series capacitors share charge but parallel ones share voltage.** In series the
same charge is displaced through every capacitor ✓ in parallel they are connected to
the same two nodes and so must have the same potential difference ✓ Reversing the two
rules is the commonest error in capacitor networks.
**Why capacitors in series add like resistors in parallel.** 1/C_total = Σ1/C ✓ exactly
the reciprocal of the resistor rules - a useful symmetry to remember.
**Reading the distractors.** **36 µC** ✗ is the **total** charge, which belongs to the
6 µF capacitor. **12 µC** ✗ is the charge on the **2 µF**. **6 µC** ✗ matches no element
✓ Each distractor is a real quantity in this circuit, answering a different question.
∴ 24 × 10⁻⁶ C.

Differentiate the potential and change the sign.
**Step 1 — apply E = −dV/dx.** With V = 3x²:
dV/dx = **6x**
E_x = **−6x** ✓
**Step 2 — substitute x = 2 m.**
E = −6(2)
= **−12 V m⁻¹** ✓
**Why the other coordinates do not matter.** V depends on x alone, so
E_y = −∂V/∂y = **0** and E_z = **0** ✓
The y = 0 and z = 1 m in the question are there only to test whether that is seen; the
field is wholly along x.
**What the negative sign means.** The field points along **−x**, that is **towards the
origin** ✓ Potential increases as x², so it rises steeply with x, and the field always
points **down** the potential hill - from high V to low V.
**A check by finite differences.** Near x = 2:
V(2·01) = 3(4·0401) = **12·12 V**
V(1·99) = 3(3·9601) = **11·88 V**
E_x = −(12·12 − 11·88)/0·02 = **−12 V m⁻¹** ✓ exactly.
**Why the field is not uniform.** E_x = −6x grows in magnitude with x ✓ at x = 1 it is
−6 V m⁻¹ and at x = 3 it is −18. A **uniform** field requires V linear in x; a quadratic
potential gives a linearly varying field.
**What charge distribution could produce this.** By Gauss's law in differential form,
d²V/dx² = −ρ/ε₀, and here d²V/dx² = **6** ✓ so the region contains a uniform negative
charge density ρ = −6ε₀ - a physically consistent arrangement.
**Checking the units.** 3x² with x in metres gives volts, so the 3 carries units of
V m⁻² ✓ and its derivative 6x is in **V m⁻¹**, the correct unit of field.
**Reading the distractors.** **+12 V m⁻¹** ✗ drops the minus sign in E = −dV/dx - the
commonest error. **±6 V m⁻¹** ✗ forget the factor of 2 from differentiating x² ✓
∴ − 12 V m⁻¹.

Build the combination from the dimensions of h and e and check it against resistance.
**Step 1 — find the dimensions of resistance.** From P = I²R,
[R] = [M L² T⁻³]/[A²]
= **[M L² T⁻³ A⁻²]** ✓
**Step 2 — find the dimensions of h.** From E = hν,
[h] = [M L² T⁻²]/[T⁻¹]
= **[M L² T⁻¹]** ✓
**Step 3 — find the dimensions of e.** Charge is current x time:
[e] = **[A T]** ✓
**Step 4 — test h/e².**
[h/e²] = [M L² T⁻¹]/[A² T²]
= **[M L² T⁻³ A⁻²]** ✓ exactly the dimensions of resistance.
**The numerical value.**
h/e² = 6·626 x 10⁻³⁴/(1·602 x 10⁻¹⁹)²
= **25813 Ω** ✓
**Why this number is famous.** It is the **von Klitzing constant**, R_K ✓ In the
**quantum Hall effect** the Hall resistance of a two-dimensional electron gas is
quantised in exact submultiples of it, R_H = h/(νe²) with ν an integer. The effect is so
reproducible that since 1990 it has **defined** the practical ohm, and it won von
Klitzing the 1985 Nobel Prize.
**A related dimensionless combination.** The **fine-structure constant**
α = e²/(4πε₀ℏc) ≈ **1/137** ✓ is built from the same ingredients and is a pure number -
a reminder that only particular combinations of h and e give a resistance.
**Testing the other options.**
**h/e** = [M L² T⁻¹]/[A T] = [M L² T⁻² A⁻¹] - that is **magnetic flux**, in webers ✗
**h²/e²** = [M² L⁴ T⁻² A⁻² T⁻²] - the square of a flux ✗
**h²/e** ✗ matches nothing standard
Only **h/e²** has the dimensions of resistance ✓
∴ h/e².

Newton's second law with the electric force gives the acceleration directly.
**Step 1 — write the force on the charge.**
F = qE ✓
**Step 2 — apply Newton's second law.**
F = ma
so
qE = ma
**Step 3 — solve.**
**a = qE/m** ✓
**Checking the dimensions.**
[qE] = [A T][M L T⁻³ A⁻¹] = **[M L T⁻²]** - a force ✓
dividing by [M] gives **[L T⁻²]** - an acceleration ✓
The options m/qE and q/mE both fail this test, which disposes of them without any
physics at all.
**Why a light particle accelerates more.** The acceleration is **inversely** proportional
to the mass ✓ An electron in a given field accelerates about **1836 times** faster than
a proton, which is why electron beams are so easily steered and why cathode-ray tubes
and oscilloscopes use electrons rather than ions.
**A worked value.** An electron in a field of 1000 V m⁻¹:
a = (1·6 x 10⁻¹⁹)(1000)/(9·1 x 10⁻³¹)
= **1·76 x 10¹⁴ m s⁻²** ✓
some 10¹³ times the acceleration due to gravity - which is why gravity is always
neglected in such problems.
**The direction.** For a **positive** charge the acceleration is along Ē; for a
**negative** one it is **opposite** to Ē ✓ The formula gives the magnitude in both
cases.
**What follows from a constant acceleration.** In a **uniform** field the motion obeys
the ordinary equations of kinematics ✓ A charge projected across the field therefore
traces a **parabola**, exactly like a projectile under gravity - the principle of the
cathode-ray tube's deflecting plates.
**Reading the distractors.** **mqE** ✗ multiplies by the mass instead of dividing -
it would make heavy particles accelerate faster. **m/qE** ✗ is the reciprocal, with
units of s² m⁻¹. **q/mE** ✗ has the field in the denominator, predicting **more**
acceleration in a **weaker** field ✓
∴ qE/m.

An electron is **negative**, so the force on it is **opposite** to the electric field -
and that reverses one of the four statements.
**Step 1 — test the statement about motion along the field.** The force on a charge is
F̄ = qĒ, and for an electron q = −e, so
**F̄ = −eĒ**, directed **against** the field ✓
An electron moving **in the direction of** Ē is therefore moving **against** the force on
it: it is **decelerated** and **loses** kinetic energy ✗ The statement that it gains
kinetic energy is **false** - this is the one to pick ✓
**Step 2 — check the parabolic path.** An electron shot **at right angles** to a uniform
field has constant velocity along its initial direction and uniform acceleration
perpendicular to it ✓ That is exactly the structure of projectile motion, so the path is
a **parabola** - **true**.
**Step 3 — check the electron at rest in a magnetic field.** The magnetic force is
F̄ = qv̄ x B̄, which is **zero** when v = 0 ✓ A stationary charge feels no magnetic force
at all - **true**.
**Step 4 — check the kinetic energy in a magnetic field.** The magnetic force is always
**perpendicular** to the velocity, so it does **no work** ✓
P = F̄·v̄ = q(v̄ x B̄)·v̄ = **0**
The speed, and hence the kinetic energy, is unchanged - **true**.
**The electron's trajectory in the second case.** Moving at right angles to a uniform
magnetic field, it travels in a **circle** of radius r = mv/(eB) at constant speed ✓
Direction changes continuously, energy not at all.
**The contrast between the two fields.**
**electric field**: force along (or against) Ē, **does work**, changes the speed ✓
**magnetic field**: force perpendicular to v̄, does **no work**, changes only the
direction ✓
That single distinction accounts for three of the four statements here.
**Where an electron does gain energy from a field.** When it moves **against** Ē, that
is, from low potential to high ✓ which is why an electron gun accelerates electrons
towards a **positive** anode.
∴ the statement that an electron moving in the direction of the electric field gains
kinetic energy.
